newsitem.title: ROMANIA: FEATURE - Bucharest bourse could recover with new government.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Bucharest bourse could recover with new government.

text.p: Romania's fledgling stock exchange, mired by slack trading in recent months, could get a shot in the arm if a new reformist government sends out the right signals.

Analysts say the bourse, which celebrates its first post- communist year of operation next week, will take time to recover from months of doldrums caused by poor economic performance and cash and share liquidity shortages.
But the prospect of a new administration after the centrist Democratic Convention (CDR) triumphed in general elections has generated optimism among traders and bourse officials.
"The centre-right government to be formed soon is good news for the market, which it can stimulate with proper steps," said economist Teodor Nicolaescu, who is on the bourse committee.

But officials said a cabinet consisting mainly of the CDR and the Social Democrats would have to offer lower taxes and exemptions to restore shaky confidence and appeal to local and foreign investors.
Most analysts and brokers agree dull market performance was caused by adverse macroeconomic conditions and government inaction during an election year.
"The new government should promptly address macroeconomic issues and promote privatisation and restructuring to sustain macroeconomic stabilisation," a local economist said.
The CDR campaigned on the basis of its "Contract with Romania", calling for tax cuts and support for capital markets.
All plans are on hold pending Sunday's presidential election run-off pitting ex-communist Ion Iliescu against CDR leader Emil Constantinescu.

Liberal politicians say Romania can only shake off its communist legacy if Iliescu is thrown out of office. The president says his cautious brand of reforms has saved the country from economic collapse of the sort that has afflicted neighbouring Bulgaria.
The bourse has been sluggish over the past four months with turnover averaging 50 million leu per session against peaks last spring of 1.5 billion.
Analysts say investors are scared off by the outgoing government's policy of artificially holding the leu currency well above market rates and by rises in inflation.
The leu is currently quoted at 3,460 on the interbank market but a dollar fetches up to 4,800 at exchange shops.
Inflation, beaten back to 27.8 percent last year, is running at 45 percent, well in excess of recommendations by the International Monetary Fund, which suspended credit tranches earlier this year.
"Domestic capital flows to the exchange are scarce, mainly due to investors' eroded confidence in the market after upsets in investment funds and banking sectors," Nicolaescu said.

Investment funds saw their units fall earlier this year when the capital market regulator issued new rules altering the value of their assets. Panicked investors rushed to redeem their money and two major funds were suspended for a time.
Two commercial banks ran into trouble after revealing huge losses and bad debts. Their fate -- liquidation or reorganisation -- lies with the courts.
"We have seen an exodus of savings and profits to hard currency or real estate, seen as safer placements," Nicolaescu said.
Privatisation remains the key to attracting foreign investors and boosting share liquidity.
"To make the economy appeal to foreigners, healthy assets should go on sale, with the sell-off also covering strategic units, such as lotteries and telecommunications," said an economist.
Analysts say the new government should also promote legislation on foreign portfolio investors, now subject to lengthy red tape.
"This is a sensitive area as foreign portolio investors are known to switch in and out of emerging markets," said Vivien Ashton, British Know-How Fund adviser to the stock exchange.

"This happened in Poland and Mexico, bringing volatility to these markets. One way to solve these in-and-out practices could be for the new government to offer tax benefits to those holding stock rather than trading it on a short-term basis."
The free transfer of property, almost completed under a mass sell-off launched by the outgoing government, solved the liquidity problem only partially.

The scheme offered Romanians up to 60 percent share in 4,000 state companies, with the remaining 40 percent slated for cash sales to local and foreign investors. Subscription was 60 percent or more for around 2,000 firms.

Analysts say the new cabinet should encourage the State Ownership Fund, a majority stockholder of state companies before the mass sell-off, to use exchange facilities to part with the 40 percent stake earmarked for cash sales.
"The exchange has the facilities to trade mass privatisation shares," said a bourse executive.
Treasury bills and bonds, so far offered only on the primary market, could also boost market liquidity.
"If you look at European bourses you'll see most trading is in these securities," a Western analyst said. "Also, investment fund portfolios traditionally include government bonds."
